content: Vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) is recognized as the second most common vaginal infection, following bacterial vaginosis. Probiotics have been proposed as a potential treatment for VVC due to their ability to help maintain and restore the normal vaginal microbiota and their potential to inhibit the growth of Candida species. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of probiotics in treating vulvovaginal candidiasis in non-pregnant women. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Review Group's Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, up to October 2017. Additional resources, such as the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, ClinicalTrials.gov, Web of Science, OpenGrey, specialty journals, conference proceedings, and pharmaceutical company data, were also reviewed. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included if they investigated probiotics, either alone or as an adjunct to conventional antifungal treatments, for VVC in non-pregnant women. Trials involving women with recurrent VVC, co-infections, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppressive disorders, or those taking immunosuppressive medications were excluded. Probiotics of any species, preparation type, dosage, or route of administration were eligible for inclusion. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials and extracted data. Disagreements were resolved through consensus. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. A total of 10 RCTs, involving 1656 participants, met the inclusion criteria. None of these trials were funded by the pharmaceutical industry. All studies used probiotics as an adjunct to antifungal drugs. The findings indicated that probiotics increased the rate of short-term clinical cure (risk ratio [RR] 1.14, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.05 to 1.24, 695 participants, 5 studies, low-quality evidence) and short-term mycological cure (RR 1.06, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.10, 969 participants, 7 studies, low-quality evidence). Additionally, probiotics reduced the relapse rate at one month (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.68, 388 participants, 3 studies, very low-quality evidence). However, the use of probiotics did not result in a higher frequency of long-term clinical cure. One month after treatment, the RR for long-term clinical cure was 1.07 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.33, 172 participants, 1 study, very low-quality evidence), and three months after treatment, the RR was 1.30 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.70, 172 participants, 1 study, very low-quality evidence). Similarly, probiotics did not significantly improve long-term mycological cure rates. One month after treatment, the RR for long-term mycological cure was 1.26 (95% CI 0.93 to 1.71, 627 participants, 3 studies, very low-quality evidence), and three months after treatment, the RR was 1.16 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.35, 172 participants, 1 study, very low-quality evidence). The use of probiotics did not increase the frequency of serious adverse events (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.22 to 2.94, 440 participants, 2 studies, low-quality evidence). No eligible RCTs were identified for outcomes such as time to first relapse, the need for additional treatment at the end of therapy, patient satisfaction, or cost-effectiveness. In conclusion, the evidence, which is of low and very low quality, suggests that probiotics used as an adjunct to conventional antifungal treatments may increase the rates of short-term clinical and mycological cure and reduce the relapse rate at one month. However, this benefit does not extend to long-term clinical or mycological cure. Probiotics do not appear to increase the risk of serious or non-serious adverse events. Further well-designed RCTs with standardized methodologies, larger sample sizes, and longer follow-up periods are needed to provide more robust evidence.
